law_discussed: ICT Act 2006; DSA 2018; Pornography Control Act 2012
key_findings: Sub-inspectors face internal barriers (little tech/logistics at station level, shallow cyber training, non-investigative duty load) and external ones (victim non-cooperation from shame, bKash and Facebook slow or refusing to share data, SIMs registered on others' NIDs, volatile digital evidence, cross-jurisdiction offenders).
prevalence_reported: Cites Dhaka Cyber Tribunal 2013-2020: 2,669 cases, 768 disposed, 22 convictions (2.86%); ~80% of victims unsatisfied with police (CCAF 2023) - secondary figures
author_gaps: Perspective of specialised units and victims not covered; small convenience sample
recommendations: Station-level cyber tools; cyber/digital-forensics modules in Sardah training; regular in-service training; staffing; police-private sector (MFS, platform) cooperation; curb fraudulent SIM registration
quality_note: Small sample (n=8), all male SIs, two districts; clear methods; author is criminologist (PhD on cyber violence victimisation) - possible supervisor/collaborator contact

key_findings: Curated ~50k Bangla/English/Banglish SMS (fraud vs legitimate, from Facebook scam reports and volunteers); Bangla-BERT-base best (91% accuracy, recall 100%, precision 85.5%); prototype app shows pop-up scam warnings.
author_gaps: No public Bangla fraud-SMS dataset existed; no formal user testing of alerts
recommendations: Integrate into telecom/MFS SMS filtering
quality_note: Internal inconsistencies (conclusion describes emotion detection; recall 100% for all models implausible); technical only

population: university students; police or justice actors
theory: none (trust in automation / appropriate reliance framing)
key_findings: 77% cautious about treating digital media as authentic, 64% say legal professionals need stronger deepfake-evaluation skills, 56% aware AI can fabricate media; awareness weakly/not associated with endorsing training. Argues provenance, authentication and evidentiary weight should be trained separately (Evidence Act ss 65A-65B).
author_gaps: No measure of actual detection skill; non-probability sample dominated by law students; test practitioners with case tasks; pre-post training evaluation
recommendations: Case-based legal training on provenance, preservation and interpreting forensic reports
quality_note: Same 'Group 6' dataset used in companion papers (R0022 likely) - not independent; GenAI-assisted drafting disclosed; careful statistics

key_findings: 49% recognised AI misuse for phishing/impersonation, 81% verify unusual requests, 82% use security practices; awareness not associated with protective behaviour after adjustment, daily AI use was.
author_gaps: Need validated measures and behavioural (not self-report) outcomes; prospective designs
recommendations: Distinguish recognition, detection confidence and behaviour in university cyber education
quality_note: Same 'Group 6' dataset as R0015 - not independent sample

key_findings: XGBoost best on synthetic PaySim mobile-money data (F1 0.54, PR-AUC 0.57); calibration and SHAP explanations; top-1% adaptive alerting cuts false positives 39% but halves recall.
author_gaps: No real Bangladeshi MFS/bank transaction data available; validation on governed local data needed
recommendations: Bangladesh Bank e-KYC guidance should encourage chronological validation and explainable, capacity-aware alerting
quality_note: Uses NO Bangladesh data - evidence of data-access gap for MFS fraud research

key_findings: CSA 2026's vague offences ('defamatory online content', 'false information', 'cyber propaganda', 'cyber terrorism') fail ICCPR Art 19(3) legality/necessity/proportionality; ss 31-36 allow device/traffic access without judicial warrant; chilling effect; compared with US First Amendment, EU DSA and Shreya Singhal (India). Fails all five tests for sound cyber legislation.
recommendations: Five reform principles: narrow definitions, judicial warrants, proportionate penalties, independent oversight, decriminalise defamation
quality_note: Undergraduate-authored; low-tier journal (IRE); some garbled text

key_findings: Bangladesh lacks treaty networks (not party to Budapest Convention), relies on slow MLATs, has outdated digital-evidence and data-access procedures; compared with US CLOUD Act and EU EIO/e-Evidence, causing investigative delays in transnational cases (e.g. 2016 Bangladesh Bank heist).
recommendations: Harmonised cybercrime definitions; streamlined MLATs; digital evidence reform; capacity building; accede to Budapest Convention
quality_note: Secondary sources only

location: national (comparative: EU, Italy, UK, US, China, S Korea, India, Bangladesh)
law_discussed: CSA 2026 / Ordinance 2025 (as coded in index); Pornography Control Act 2012
key_findings: Leximetric Synthetic Media Legal Coverage Index: Bangladesh scored lowest (6/18, 33%) vs US 15/18; sexual-deepfake offences widely covered, likeness/licensing rights least. Proposes four-layer model (right, licence, transparency, liability) for Bangladesh.
recommendations: Dignity-based personality right with copyright as enforcement container; transparency and platform duties
quality_note: Author based in India; journal (Int J Special Education) off-topic outlet; Bangladesh is one of 8 cases but scored and targeted by recommendations

key_findings: 2017 India-Bangladesh CERT MoU (CERT-In / BGD e-GOV CIRT) is weak because Art 5 defers to divergent national laws; no binding standards, oversight or law-enforcement integration. Proposes AI tools for harmonisation and joint threat intelligence.
prevalence_reported: Cites secondary figures: DMP 2023 23.9% of cyber cases Facebook breaches/extortion/fraud; '73% of Bangladeshi women experienced cybercrime' (unsourced)
recommendations: Operationalise MoU Art 5 with joint protocols, cyber exercises, shared AI-based threat classification and evidence standards
quality_note: Indian political science author; low-tier journal; largely descriptive, weakly sourced statistics

key_findings: DSA 2018 (and Nigeria's Cybercrimes Act 2015) use vague offences ('false', 'offensive', 'defamatory') enabling selective enforcement against journalists/activists; misinformation used to justify censorship; opaque state-platform takedowns; Bangladesh enforcement more centralised and systematic than Nigeria's.
author_gaps: Desk-based; no interviews or enforcement data
recommendations: Narrow definitions; independent multi-stakeholder digital regulator; platform transparency; media literacy over punishment; rights-based data protection
quality_note: Nigerian ICT agency authors; several references look unverifiable (possible fabricated citations); secondary sources only

key_findings: 55% see AI misuse as 'very common', women and children seen as most vulnerable; 65% think current laws inadequate for AI harms; two deepfake harassment/blackmail cases show barriers to justice. Calls AI harms a 'legal response gap'.
recommendations: Victim-centred legal reform, digital forensic capacity, AI liability rules, AI governance framework, digital literacy
quality_note: Perception survey (not victimisation); sampling not specified; low-tier journal

key_findings: Three forms: identity-based (body shaming, gender-nonconforming students labelled, regional accents), interactional aggression (sarcasm, exclusion of high achievers), technologically mediated manipulation (fake profiles sending fake nudes to family, deepfakes, doxing, strategic tagging). Memes/GIFs/emojis disguise hostility as humour. Most victims never report (fear of retaliation, privacy, futility).
author_gaps: Quantitative measurement of instances and impacts needed
recommendations: Anonymous campus reporting, anti-retaliation policy, peer support, teacher training, disciplinary action
quality_note: Good qualitative victim data; linguistics not criminology; purposive sample

key_findings: CSA 2026 lacks clear definitions and an ethical basis for AI-driven defamation/deepfakes; proposes codifying digital defamation via Islamic principles (Hifz al-Ird), discretionary (ta'zir) restorative punishment, and protecting sincere political criticism (nasiha).
recommendations: Shariah-informed definitions of digital defamation; restorative justice for deepfake victims; protect constructive criticism
quality_note: Written in Bangla (legacy SutonnyMJ font, text garbled in extraction); Islamic Studies authors; normative

key_findings: Lists attacks on Bangladeshi critical infrastructure (Sonali Bank 2013, Bangladesh Bank 2016, BPDB 2015, WannaCry at BERC 2017, DESCO prepaid-meter hack of 18,000 meters, Biman ransomware, Standard Chartered card fraud 2025); incidents under-reported and opaque. Compares US/UK/EU public-private partnership models.
recommendations: National Cyber Security Commission; PPP information sharing; transparent incident reporting; awareness campaigns
quality_note: Borderline (infrastructure security more than crime); relies heavily on one newspaper source (Wahid 2025); literature-only

key_findings: Mainly physical, psychological and financial COVID-era safety; DSA appears only briefly (one interviewee quote; cites Article 19: 60 DSA cases against 100 people incl. 22 journalists in Jan-May 2020).
prevalence_reported: Secondary: Article 19 2020 - 60 DSA cases, 100 people, 22 journalists
recommendations: nr
quality_note: Excluded at full text: DSA is a minor theme. Article 19 figure useful as background

key_findings: Digital evidence in general (Evidence (Amendment) Act 2022 s65B) assessed against Islamic evidentiary principles; proposes Shariah-Compliant Digital Evidence Framework. Not tied to cybercrime cases.
author_gaps: Empirical study of digital evidence use in courts; deepfake identification
recommendations: nr
quality_note: Excluded at full text: digital evidence in general, not cybercrime (per rule)

key_findings: All defamation is criminal in Bangladesh with no public/private figure distinction; DSA online defamation provisions allowed warrantless arrest and device seizure and were used against journalists, academics and opponents (many cases 2020-21), chilling debate.
recommendations: Decriminalise defamation; serious-harm threshold; public-figure 'actual malice' doctrine
quality_note: Dhaka University Law Journal (reputable domestic)

location: Bogura; Rangpur; Natore; Sirajganj; Jamalpur; Rajshahi
key_findings: Delivery fraud against sellers (fake cash-on-delivery orders, refusals, fake returns) was the most consistent harm reported by all rural women F-commerce sellers; losses borne entirely by seller, no recourse against buyer or courier; coping = advance payment, blocking. Online harassment mainly from male customers adds emotional stress and triggers household suspicion; bKash/Nagad accounts often controlled by male relatives.
author_gaps: Urban-rural comparison; quantitative impact studies; platform algorithm effects
recommendations: Grievance redress for delivery fraud with couriers/platforms; Meta scam-profile warnings and reporting; collateral-free credit; digital rights training
quality_note: Seller-side fraud victimisation is rarely studied - useful gap evidence

key_findings: Comparative policy analysis on 5 dimensions; Bangladesh's NCSS 2023 judged more operationally detailed than Pakistan's 2021 NCSP (cybercrime units, reporting portal, MLATs); Pakistan's PECA criticised as speech-focused; both lack victim protection for individuals and e-commerce users.
recommendations: Funded research agenda, PPP mechanisms, curriculum integration, victim protection (directed at Pakistan)
quality_note: Pakistani author; treats Bangladesh mainly as benchmark; some claims about Bangladesh (e.g. MLAT partnerships) contradict R0039 - descriptive, uncritical of DSA

key_findings: Nationally representative: 6.6% of adolescents reported cyberbullying (verbal 31.6%, physical 20.8%); cyberbullying independently associated with higher depressive symptoms (b=1.15, p=0.012); cumulative bullying exposure shows graded association. No significant gender interaction for cyberbullying.
prevalence_reported: Cyberbullying victimisation 6.60% among 15-19 year olds (BAHWS 2019-20, n=9,116) - contrasts with ~32% in small convenience samples
recommendations: Comprehensive bullying prevention including online; accessible psychosocial services
quality_note: KEY PAPER: only nationally representative cyber-victimisation estimate so far; PLOS Mental Health; secondary analysis of public dataset (BAHWS) - usable for PhD

theory: none (crime prevention framing; notes lack of theory in Bangladesh prevention)
key_findings: Bangladesh scams dominated by institutional financial scams (e-commerce firms like Evaly, politically connected actors) with reactive, slow enforcement and no dedicated law; Singapore uses community interventions (ScamShield, anti-scam centre) against purchase, romance and impersonation scams.
author_gaps: Need for theoretical frameworks for scam prevention in Bangladesh
recommendations: Adopt Singapore-style anti-scam centre, public-private alerts, community awareness; dedicated anti-fraud law
quality_note: Dhaka University Studies with NUS/SIT co-authors; literature-only; conflates corporate e-commerce fraud with online scams

key_findings: Narrative synthesis of student cyber-awareness studies (India, Turkey, Indonesia etc.): awareness high, training and protective behaviour low.
recommendations: nr
quality_note: Excluded at full text: Pakistani authors, general international review; no Bangladesh analysis

key_findings: Descriptive account of cybercrime's economic cost and a speculative section on threats to environmental data; claims CIRT incidents rose from 10,500 (2019) to 24,600 (2023) and annual losses of BDT 500-600 crore.
prevalence_reported: Claimed CIRT incident counts 2019-2023 and BDT 500-600 crore annual loss - unverifiable
recommendations: Cyber security budget, SME support, DSA reform, international cooperation
quality_note: LOW QUALITY: rounded statistics not traceable to CIRT publications; several references appear fabricated; off-topic journal (Int J Environmental Sciences). Do not cite figures.

law_discussed: none (regulators: Bangladesh Bank, BTRC, Digital Security Agency)
key_findings: Case study of 2025 Standard Chartered OTP/SIM-swap scam: fraud arose at interfaces between banks, MFS, telcos and regulators; each actor 'followed protocol', victims left with blame-shifting; even educated users deceived by impersonation of bank officials. Proposes Multi-Actor Accountability Framework.
author_gaps: Quantitative modelling of fraud propagation; why informed users are deceived; evaluation of cross-institutional coordination
recommendations: Unified fraud reporting protocol; national digital-finance fraud intelligence platform; joint cyber-finance task force; shared liability
quality_note: Secondary/news-based case study; low-tier journal; useful conceptual framing of MFS/bank fraud governance gap

key_findings: Claims 27% could recognise phishing, 42% encountered attempts, 14% compromised (mainly fake job/scholarship offers), mean loss BDT 4,800; victims felt shame, withdrew online, rarely reported (stigma, distrust of justice).
recommendations: Curriculum cyber education, campaigns, victim support centres, legal reform, police training
quality_note: LOW QUALITY: very thin methods/results, no tables; same authors as R0141; several Bangladesh references appear fabricated (e.g. 'Journal of Digital Trust'); treat figures with caution

law_discussed: ICT Act 2006; Consumer Protection Act 2009; Penal Code; Digital Commerce Operation Guidelines 2018
key_findings: E-commerce fraud (advance-payment Facebook page scams, non-delivery, fake goods; complaints against Evaly etc.) surged after COVID; fragmented laws (Contract, Sale of Goods, Consumer Protection, ICT Act) with no dedicated e-commerce law; DNCRP complaints doubled.
recommendations: Dedicated e-commerce/online shopping law; amend Consumer Protection Act to name e-commerce; cyber courts; licensing of Facebook sellers
quality_note: Jahangirnagar Review (domestic); descriptive, news-based

key_findings: Professionals rate outdated laws as the biggest obstacle (mean 4.3/5); few extradition treaties, little evidence sharing, MLATs rarely effective, JITs hard to form; forensic labs, encryption and investigator training weak.
author_gaps: Victim voices and comparative analysis missing; qualitative depth needed
recommendations: Law reform aligned to international norms, cyber courts, forensic labs, investigator/judge training, victim legal aid
quality_note: Descriptive Likert means only; some implausible statistics (median 43, SD 5.0) suggest careless reporting; new journal (IJCJ vol 1)

law_discussed: CSA 2023; DSA 2018; draft Personal Data Protection Act 2023
key_findings: CSA 2023 and draft data protection law lack consent standards, breach notification, clear limits on speech provisions and investigative capacity; benchmarked against GDPR and Budapest Convention.
recommendations: Comprehensive data protection law, breach notification duty, narrow speech offences, investigation capacity, accede to Budapest Convention
quality_note: Desk-based; translated text with errors (e.g. 'solar safety'); some news sources

key_findings: 90.5% of 295 DU students reported at least one form of cyber-victimisation (CYVIC 19-item scale, Bangla); 'often/always': social media ignoring 13.9%, offensive comments 12.4%, impersonation 7.9%, private images shared 4.5%, sextortion/blackmail with intimate material 2.6%, nude images recorded and shared 2.2%. No significant gender difference overall.
prevalence_reported: Any cyber-victimisation 90.5% (n=295, convenience sample); intimate-image blackmail 2.6% often/always, 18.4% rarely
recommendations: University anti-bullying policies, confidential reporting, counselling and peer support
quality_note: Validated scale; open data on OSF; convenience sample, single university; uses 'excluded non-victims' design oddly

key_findings: Fintech adoption and bank cybersecurity readiness overview; fraud only as a generic risk. Claims a 315-person survey but reports no results tables.
recommendations: nr
quality_note: Excluded at full text: fintech/security readiness, not crime; claimed methods not reported; several references appear fabricated

key_findings: Press freedom coverage during 2013 Shahbag period; Islamist groups most-cited barrier; social media central to coverage. No analysis of cyber laws or cyber offences.
recommendations: nr
quality_note: Excluded at full text: press freedom generally; appears recycled from an older (c.2014) study

key_findings: Inconsistent protective behaviour: most don't use 2FA, rarely update browsers or check privacy settings, many neutral on sharing personal info/accepting strangers; password, browser and social media practices each correlate with overall awareness.
prevalence_reported: none (no victimisation measured); cites Cyber Tribunal ~4,500 cases 2013-2021, mostly acquittals (bdnews24)
author_gaps: Small single-university sample; qualitative methods needed
recommendations: Curriculum cyber hygiene, workshops, password guidance
quality_note: Tag: awareness. Purposive sample at BUP; awareness outcome circularly built from same items

law_discussed: Prevention and Suppression of Human Trafficking Act 2012; ICT Act 2006; CSA 2023; Penal Code
key_findings: 'Cyber slavery': Bangladeshis recruited via Facebook/TikTok/Telegram fake job ads and trafficked to Southeast Asian scam compounds, forced to run online fraud under torture; no law explicitly covers it - trafficking and cybercrime laws do not connect.
recommendations: Amend anti-trafficking law for online recruitment/digital coercion; regulate online job recruitment; joint trafficking-cyber units; victim rehabilitation
quality_note: Short, news-based. NEW THEME: scam-compound trafficking (victim-offender overlap) - emerging gap with almost no empirical research

key_findings: Among medical students, 48.3% reported cyberbullying victimisation (any frequency) and 39.5% admitted cyberbullying others; verbal (82%) and physical (73%) bullying more common; hostel environment, weak administration and student politics key drivers.
prevalence_reported: Cyberbullying victimisation 48.3%, perpetration 39.5% (n=632 medical students, convenience)
recommendations: Hostel supervision, reporting channels, counselling, enforcement
quality_note: Included at full text because it reports cyberbullying prevalence (rule for mental-health/bullying papers); rare perpetration figure; weak reporting (inconsistent percentages)

key_findings: Synthesises TF-VAW evidence: ActionAid 2022 - 63.5% of women harassed online; 78.7% TF-VAW (2025 roundtable); Ordinance 2025 s25 first defines sextortion, revenge porn, CSAM with enhanced penalties for women/children; Police Cyber Support for Women received 43,834 complaints to Feb 2025 but most victims don't file cases; rural women face access gap plus blackmail.
prevalence_reported: Secondary: 63.51% women harassed online (ActionAid 2022); PCSW 43,834 complaints 2020-Feb 2025
author_gaps: Research on distinct urban/rural women's needs
recommendations: Train police on Ordinance; anonymous reporting (USSD, drop boxes); digital safety help desks; digital ethics for boys/men; cyber clubs
quality_note: Short bulletin article; useful compilation of grey-literature statistics (PCSW complaint count is valuable administrative figure)

key_findings: Interpretive policy/discourse analysis: Bangladesh's cybersecurity narrative equates resilience with regime stability and reputation management (post-2016 heist, data breaches); ICT Act and DSA internalise state-centric control norms over transparency and citizen trust; ISO 27001/NIST adopted symbolically.
recommendations: Reframe cybersecurity around institutional legitimacy, social trust and professional identity
quality_note: Theory-driven (IR constructivism) - rare; Macquarie-based author

key_findings: Vulnerability assessment/penetration testing of 20 public and private university web infrastructures: widespread vulnerabilities, private universities more vulnerable; budget neglect makes universities a 'hacker playground'.
recommendations: Security hardening, regular VAPT, budget for university IT security
quality_note: Technical only (Tier A any field); Scopus-indexed journal

key_findings: Cybersecurity risk management in Islamic banks vs international standards; fraud and attacks only as generic risks (interviews mentioned in abstract only).
recommendations: nr
quality_note: Excluded at full text: organisational security readiness, not crime (consistent with R0175)

key_findings: Internet use and adolescent wellbeing post-COVID; cyberbullying mentioned only twice (abstract, literature), no measurement.
recommendations: nr
quality_note: Excluded at full text: cyberbullying not measured (rule for mental-health papers)

location: international (India focus; Bangladesh Bank heist one of 4 cases)
key_findings: General review of financial-sector cyber threats; Bangladesh Bank heist one short case among Capital One, Equifax, Upstox.
recommendations: nr
quality_note: Excluded at full text: Indian author, generic review; Bangladesh one brief case (rule)

key_findings: Perceptions of Islamic law for preventing youth 'social crimes' (drugs, delinquency); cybercrime is one Likert item (mean 2.89).
recommendations: nr
quality_note: Excluded at full text: cybercrime one item in a list

theory: shrinking civic space; Mill's harm principle; Habermas' public sphere
key_findings: Vague cyber laws in Nepal (ETA, Social Media Bill), India (IT Act, UAPA) and Bangladesh (DSA, Ordinance) weaponised against journalists/activists (e.g. Mushtaq Ahmed died in custody under DSA); shutdowns, surveillance, platform censorship and criminal defamation form regional digital authoritarianism; violates ICCPR Art 19.
recommendations: Narrow definitions, judicial oversight, decriminalise defamation, regional digital-rights cooperation
quality_note: Nepali digital-rights practitioners; Bangladesh one of three substantive cases

sample_size: ~20 Bangladeshi + ~20 Indian interviewees; surveys; TikTok video content analysis
key_findings: UIUC PhD dissertation: Bangladeshi and Indian users perceive targeted ads through cultural/religious norms and are highly concerned about fraudulent ads; separate chapters analyse scam content on TikTok and GenAI-amplified fraud.
author_gaps: Non-Western users understudied in platform safety research
recommendations: Culture-aware platform design and ad/scam governance
quality_note: Borderline: Bangladesh is one of two interview samples; scam chapters not Bangladesh-specific. High-quality US dissertation

key_findings: Cyber-secure e-governance for SDG delivery; Bangladesh one of three cases; focus on governance architecture, not crime.
recommendations: nr
quality_note: Excluded at full text: e-governance security, not cybercrime; Indian authors, edited IIP volume

sample_size: 18 (12 rural fraud victims, 5 agents, 1 fintech expert)
key_findings: Rural MFS fraud victims depend on agents/relatives (sharing PINs), fall for calls impersonating MFS staff offering lower fees, SIM-swap fraud; little fraud-prevention knowledge; redress slow so small losses go unreported; agents and community leaders seen as key.
author_gaps: Larger quantitative and longitudinal studies; gender/income comparisons
recommendations: User-centred MFS interfaces, in-app fraud literacy, 2FA and alerts, stricter KYC (accounts on relatives' IDs), fraud response units
quality_note: RARE: primary data from MFS fraud victims (n=12) - but small, low-tier venue (Userhub)

sample_size: 1,410 DSA cases (4,404 accused) + 10 accused case studies
key_findings: CGS database of 1,410 DSA cases: 4,404 accused, 1,519 arrested (23.5 cases/month); average 3.12 accused per case - extrapolated to govt's 7,001 cases gives ~21,867 accused and ~7,542 arrested; police refuse to share data even under RTI; 10 case studies of accused show prolonged pre-trial detention, bail denial, financial ruin, social stigma; Mushtaq Ahmed died in custody.
prevalence_reported: 1,410 documented DSA cases, 4,404 accused, 1,519 arrests (Oct 2018-Sep 2023); govt figure 7,001 cases to Jan 2023
author_gaps: Official data withheld; cyber-tribunal data only covers trial stage
recommendations: Repeal DSA, release detainees, withdraw cases, transparency on case data
quality_note: KEY SOURCE: Ali Riaz/CGS (NED-funded) - the only systematic case dataset on cyber-law enforcement; grey literature; accused-side perspective

key_findings: Teenagers' perceptions of cybercrime consequences (88% loss of trust in transactions, 81% economic loss) and of cybercriminals' lifestyle (82% 'spend money lavishly', 67% 'ride the best cars'); social network users seen as prime victims (93%).
recommendations: Public-private partnership, enforce existing laws
quality_note: Police Staff College author; very weak design (accidental sample, yes/no perception items), predatory outlet (J Clinical & Laboratory Research)

key_findings: In Bangla: Islamic guidance against cyberbullying; compiles Cyber Crime Awareness Foundation figures (cyberbullying 50.27% of cybercrime victims in 2023; account hacking 28.31%; 3.25% of victims died by suicide, 21% hid incidents) and PCSW (17,280 women contacted in first year); CSA 2023 provisions listed.
recommendations: Religious-moral education, blocking harmful sites, stricter law enforcement
quality_note: Bangla, SutonnyMJ font; normative; useful compilation of CCAF annual-report figures (a recurring NGO data source worth obtaining)

key_findings: Of 60 news posts on cyberbullying against women on outlet Facebook pages, 60% framed unfavourably to victims; 25% entertainment-framed, 20% crime; celebrities (30%) and police (15%) main sources, victims only 5%.
prevalence_reported: Cites DMP 2020: 80% of cyberbullying victims are women aged 14-22; BLAST 2017: 73% of women faced online harassment
recommendations: Victim-centred media coverage and awareness role
quality_note: UGC-funded; small purposive sample; relevant to media-as-data limitations

theory: feminist theory; stress and coping theory
key_findings: All 90 purposively sampled female students reported online harassment; inappropriate comments 83%, stalking 51%, sexual harassment 42%, threats 36%, hacking/impersonation 24%; Facebook 88%, Messenger 74%; sleep disturbance 49% moderate+, suicidal thoughts 3.3%.
prevalence_reported: 100% victimisation (purposive n=90 - not a prevalence estimate)
recommendations: Cyberbullying policies in institutions, counselling, helplines, platform accountability, regular surveys
quality_note: Co-author is CID Additional DIG (police link). Purposive sample of victims inflates 'prevalence'; frequency table internally inconsistent

theory: routine activity theory; lifestyle-exposure theory; cyber-lifestyle routine activities (Reyns)
key_findings: Typology of women's victimisation on social networking sites in Bangladesh (cyberbullying, morphing, Facebook cloning, account hacking, intimate-image blackmail, hidden cameras, romance fraud, 'virtual rape'); causes: oversharing, weak privacy settings, inadequate laws, platform non-response; explained through RAT/lifestyle theory (suitable targets, absent guardianship).
prevalence_reported: Secondary: BNWLA 2014 - 65 suicide attempts by female victims 2010-14; >17,000 telecom complaints by Dec 2017, 70% from women
author_gaps: Few Bangladesh studies on causes and patterns of women's SNS victimisation
recommendations: Privacy awareness, report to cyber police, platform action
quality_note: FIRST paper to apply criminological theory (RAT/lifestyle) - but only conceptually, no data; victim-blaming language ('soft-mentality'); author is victimology PhD researcher at DU

key_findings: Claimed PRISMA-based review plus survey/interviews on sector-wide impacts of cybercrime (banking, finance) in Bangladesh; motives classified as financial, political, espionage; legal frameworks judged inadequate.
recommendations: Strengthen law enforcement capacity and cybersecurity measures
quality_note: IMPORTANT for our review: an earlier 'PRISMA' review of Bangladesh cybercrime exists - must be cited and differentiated (ours is a scoping review with transparent search and charting). Methods vague; predatory-leaning publisher (Learning Gate)

law_discussed: Bangladesh Bank MFS Regulations 2022; Money Laundering Prevention Act 2012
key_findings: Bangladesh Bank MFS regulations rely on weak KYC (anyone with another person's NID details can access/open accounts) and a reactive risk-based model, enabling MFS fraud and illicit financial flows (IFF).
recommendations: Smart regulation; stronger e-KYC/biometric verification; proactive supervision
quality_note: Univ. of Pecs yearbook (Hungary); cited by R0239. Links MFS fraud to KYC/NID misuse - same mechanism police describe in R0241

key_findings: Case studies of Shahidul Alam (detained), cartoonist Ahmed Kabir Kishore (custodial torture), Mushtaq Ahmed (custodial death) and filmmaker Saddam Hossen show ICT s57 -> DSA -> CSA used to silence academics, journalists and artists, producing a culture of fear.
recommendations: Repeal/reform speech provisions; protect dissent
quality_note: Indiana University PhD student; SCIRP journal; case-based

key_findings: Overview of white-collar crime (embezzlement, corruption, money laundering); cybercrime/digital fraud one item among several.
recommendations: nr
quality_note: Excluded at full text: cybercrime one item in a list; low-tier journal

theory: none (regime type / spiral of silence framing)
key_findings: Survey of Facebook users incl. journalists, opposition activists, academics: restrictive regime structure and DSA increase self-censorship; higher education associated with more self-censorship; 'climate of fear' x critical content interaction intensifies it; gender minimal effect.
recommendations: Legal reform for free expression
quality_note: Univ. of Bergen author; small purposive sample; quantitative evidence on chilling effect (rare)

key_findings: NLP sentiment model for AML/CFT adverse-media screening in an MFS (94.6% weighted accuracy); about money laundering compliance, not cybercrime.
recommendations: nr
quality_note: Excluded at full text: AML compliance tool, not cybercrime

population: general public; police or justice actors
sample_size: 50 (public, people involved in scams, police - breakdown not reported)
location: nr (mentions Madhupur-Tangail, Gazipur, Dhaka scam hubs)
key_findings: Romance scams rising; claims interviews with victims, people involved in scams and police; scammers clustered in Madhupur (Tangail), Gazipur, Dhaka; victims ashamed to report; laws lack a romance-fraud offence; police lack training and tools for transnational cases.
recommendations: Define online dating fraud in law, train police, public awareness
quality_note: Only paper so far claiming OFFENDER interviews - but methods written in future tense, results only report demographics (n=50, low-income, low-education); thematic findings not shown. New journal (vol 1)

key_findings: Trolling used to embarrass, intimidate and silence TV actors, theatre performers and rural artists in Bangladesh; causes psychological distress, depression and alienation; framed as human rights violation.
recommendations: Empower artists, platform moderation, supportive digital environment
quality_note: Small sample; international author team (India, Bangladesh, Saudi Arabia); new victim group (artists)

key_findings: Anthropology of mobile phone regulation, SIM registration and cybercrime legislation in Papua New Guinea.
recommendations: nr
quality_note: Excluded at full text: PNG study; Bangladesh only cited (Huang 2017)
